signals.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
signals.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. signals.title: Out There
signals.description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. In a place you know, reflect on “ what that place has witnessed , remembered, celebrated, protected, or survived. … If this river, tree, park, or wooded pathway could talk — tell us poems, tell us stories — what do you think it would say?” Write about it. Leave a comment THERE’S MORE! In connection with Write Out, there are two online events that sound cool: Hawaiian Kilo: Writing Rooted in Place Native Hawaiians developed a practice known as Kilo — “to watch, observe, examine, or forecast.” This means closely observing the natural world and its patterns, ideally to better steward the environment. A Zoom workshop, “led by teachers from the Waiākea Intermediate School in Hilo Hawai'i,” happens October 13, 2026, 6 pm US Central time . Details and (free) registration here . Haiku + Comic = Haikomic The Write Time with Write Out Ambassador Grant Snider on October 20 . Snider is a writer/artist who combines haiku with comics. (Details on that here , and at his newsletter. ) And he is this year’s Write Out Author Ambassador. Check the Write Out newsletter for event details as they emerge. I really like the sound of this and hope to revisit. Grant Snider, via Incidental Comics Leave a comment PS I was a Write Out Ambassador last year. I love Write Out! Then you should join the community of TAoN Supporters! You’ll get access to the full archives as well as Supporter-only bonus posts and threads. Your support makes this newsletter possible. Seriously. Thank you! Subscribe now THE NEXT FREE EDITION IN TWO WEEKS! IN OTHER NEWS David Lee Roth , EMT . “ Reading Maps plots the routes characters travel in novels and films — you can trace the Pequod’s ocean path as it chases Moby Dick, or Victor Frankenstein’s pursuit of his monster from Geneva to the Arctic.” — Recomendo Lighthouses of the World , a digital map. Via Popular Science . “What Gertrude Stein, T. S. Eliot and Joan Didion Really Meant With Their Most Famous Aphorisms .” The International Dada Archive collects scanned Dada pamphlets from the early 20th century. Mark Frauenfelder found one in English called The Blind Man , co-edited by Marcel Duchamp. Its second issue, from 1917, covered the controversy around Duchamp’s Fountain , a urinal he submitted under the name Richard Mutt to the Society of Independent Artists exhibition. More from Mark here . Shadows . Via Street Art Utopia. Tobie Tse “combines hand-stitched textiles, illustration and digital motion to create visual responses to music.” Tom Waits spoken word piece : OKAY THAT’S IT! visualFeast.title: Designer Portraits: Susan Kare ⌘ The woman who gave the computer a face
visualFeast.description: Good design is not about what medium you are working in. It’s about thinking hard about what you want to do and what you have to work with before you start. — SK Susan Kare joined Apple in 1982 as the sole creator of screen graphics in the Macintosh group. As the designer “ who gave the Macintosh a smile ” she is best known for developing the distinctive icons, typefaces, and other pixel elements that gave the Macintosh its characteristic look and feel. A sculptor picks up graph paper In 1982, Susan Kare was living in the Bay Area, welding a life-size razorback hog for a museum in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Her father, Morley Richard Kare, had founded the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, spending his career studying taste and smell. His daughter had a PhD from NYU, a background in sculpture and fine art, and zero experience with computers. Then Andy Hertzfeld called. Hertzfeld and Kare had known each other since they were fourteen, classmates at Harriton High School outside Philadelphia. He was now the lead software architect on a secret project at Apple: the Macintosh. He needed someone to design the icons and typefaces for its screen. He told her if she got some graph paper, she could make small images. Kare went to the University Art supply store in Palo Alto and bought a $2.50 sketchbook. That sketchbook now sits in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Susan Kare. Apple Macintosh OS icon sketchbook. 1982 — MoMa She went to the Palo Alto public library, checked out every book she could find on typography, and brought them to the interview to prove she knew something about type. “I went into it totally green” she said later. Apple offered her a fixed-length contract to design fonts and icons. In January 1983, she started working at Apple. Her business card read “Macintosh Artist.” Susan Kare, Apple's “Macintosh Artist” relaxes at her desk in 1984. Photographer: Norman Seeff 1,024 squares The Macintosh used a bit-mapped display. The display controlled every pixel on screen. Kare’s canvas was a 32-by-32 pixel grid. 1,024 squares to communicate a single idea. She understood the constraint immediately. “Bitmap graphics are like mosaics and needlepoint and other pseudo-digital art forms, all of which I had practiced before going to Apple,” she said. “I didn’t have any computer experience, but I had experience in graphic design.” No icon editor existed when she started. She learned to calculate the hex equivalent of her pixel drawings so Hertzfeld could keyboard them into the prototype. He built her a proper editor that generated hex values under the icons. Eventually she used MacPaint itself to create icons. A MacPaint screenshot featuring Kare’s artistry, 1983. Notice the icon menu at left and the Chicago system font used for the pull-down menus. Some icons already existed from the Lisa, Apple’s earlier computer. The arrow cursor. The document with a folded corner. The trash can. The Lisa’s interface was functional but clinical, icons designed by engineers to label functions, not to invite use. It also used non-square pixels, so every element needed reworking for the Mac’s display. Kare refined the trash can. She created the application icon, a hand holding a pencil against a diamond shape, to distinguish apps from documents. She designed the Happy Mac, the smiling face that greeted users at startup. She designed the ticking bomb that appeared during system failures. For the copy function, she tried drawing a photocopier. Then she drew a cat looking in a mirror. Copy cat. She scrapped it because it wouldn’t translate internationally. The lasso, the paint bucket, the paintbrush. Each icon went through rounds of sketching on graph paper before touching a screen. Her process was the same as any visual designer working in any medium in any century. Pencil, paper, iteration. The screen was just the final surface. Kare's Happy Macintosh icon appeared at startup, greeting users with a smile to let them know everything was okay. She designed warmth into a machine. Fonts in 9 by 7 dots Most digital typefaces in 1983 were monospaced. Every character occupied the same width. Kare wanted proportional fonts, letters that breathed according to their natural shape. Each letter had to fit in a grid of 9 by 7 dots. The bold system font started as “Elefont.” It became Chicago, the typeface that would appear on the Macintosh and later the iPod for over twenty years. Kare and Hertzfeld named the early fonts after commuter train stops on Philadelphia’s Main Line: Overbrook, Merion, Ardmore, Rosemont, Paoli. Steve Jobs told them the names were too parochial. He wanted world-class cities. The fonts became New York, Geneva, London, Toronto, Venice. One font, Ransom, looked like cutout letters from a kidnapper’s note. Jobs renamed it San Francisco. Another, Cairo, featured tiny pictograms: a palm tree, a crescent moon, a skateboard. Decades before Apple introduced emoji, Kare had already drawn proto-emojis into a font. The command key and the Swedish campground ⌘ Every keyboard needs a modifier key. The Mac team struggled to find the right symbol for theirs. Kare found the answer in Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook, a reference she kept at her desk at Apple. The symbol marked interesting features on Swedish campgrounds. It was abstract enough to work as a keyboard glyph, meaningful enough to carry intention. It became ⌘, one of the most recognized symbols in computing. The pirate flag Steve Jobs liked to tell the Mac team: “ It’s better to be a pirate than join the navy. ” When the team moved into a new building, Bandley 3 , programmer Steve Capps wanted a flag. He asked Kare to design one. She drew a Jolly Roger with the eyepatch replaced by Apple’s rainbow logo. They flew it over the entrance. It stayed there for over a year. At one point, the Lisa team stole it. In 2016, Apple flew the flag again to mark the company’s 40th anniversary. This wallpape r is a nod to the Jolly Roger that flew over Bandley 3 in 1983, the building the Mac team worked in as they put the finishing touches on the Macintosh. Apple recently flew a recreation of the original 1983 flag in 2016 , when it celebrated its 40th anniversary on April 1st, shortly before moving its HQ from Infinite Loop to Apple Park. And the flag is still available on Susan Kare's website . After the Mac The Macintosh shipped in January 1984. The entire visual language Kare created came from roughly one year of work. When Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985, Kare followed him to NeXT as creative director. She was one of the company’s first ten employees. At NeXT, she connected Jobs with one of her design heroes. Kare was a devoted Paul Rand fan. She introduced Jobs to Rand’s books, and together they hired Rand to design the NeXT logo. Kare and David Kelley visited Rand at his studio. Rand, then in his seventies, told them: “I’ve been doing this for fifty-five years, and I know what you should do.” Susan Kare, center, was a creative director at NeXT, and she left with Jobs after his ouster at Apple. Kim Jenkins, right, was a key member of the NeXT marketing team. Kare founded her own studio, Susan Kare LLP, in 1989. Over the next three decades, she designed interface elements for Microsoft, Oracle, Facebook, IBM, and Sony Pictures. She designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. In 2003, she served on the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, designing coins for the United States Mint. In 2015, she joined Pinterest as product design lead. In 2018, AIGA awarded her the AIGA Medal, one of the profession’s highest honors. Kare designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. The proof of concept The Museum of Modern Art calls Kare “a pioneering and influential computer iconographer.” The label misses the point. She made the Macintosh feel human and had never touched a computer before Apple hired her. She came from sculpture, fine art, mosaics, needlepoint. She treated the pixel grid the same way she treated any design surface: as a constraint that shapes the work. “I hoped to help counter the stereotypical image of computers as cold and intimidating,” Kare said. Someone with a $2.50 sketchbook and a sculptor’s eye decided that the visual language of technology should borrow from the one humans already knew. That turned out to be enough. “I still spend my days turning dots on and off.” Today, Kare is working as a design architect at Niantic Labs and still runs her own studio in San Francisco. She sells limited-edition signed prints of her icon work, collaborates with brands like Ledger on pixel art for hardware , and her original 1982 sketchbooks remain on display at MoMA. Needlepoint to Ledger Nano™: A Conversation with Susan Kare Apple turns 50 this year. ( 50 years of thinking different. ) Researching Susan Kare felt like walking back to where it all started; reading about how she approached design problems, how she collaborated, how she used constraints to shape the work. They built the foundations of how we use computers today. They had constraints on their screens but none in their minds. I hope you enjoyed reading this one. Designer Portraits is an ongoing series about the great minds that inspire us. You can also read about Dieter Rams and Corita Kent . More portraits are on the way, follow to get notified. visualFeast.description: nas edições anteriores #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 A essa altura você já sabe que a Bits to Brands virou uma revista impressa . Duas, na verdade, considerando que estamos na segunda edição. Já somos praticamente uma banca. O que você talvez não saiba é que este processo criativo começou lá em 2014, quando a gente visualizou uma revista impressa que viria com um boné, feita para ser a companhia ideal para o verão de 2025. (Por isso a garota da capa estava sentada em uma cadeira de praia lendo uma revista, que dentro tinha uma página só de palavras cruzadas e vinha com um cartão postal retratando um dia de praia…) Ou seja: não basta selecionar os artigos, ordenar e diagramar de forma que faça sentido e pensar o projeto gráfico - toda revista precisa ter um tema. _ Na sua segunda edição, em 2026, o escolhido foi Bora de Brasil . Uma das grandes tendências do ano, e um tema de grande interesse por aqui - das pesquisas traduzindo a nossa cultura à possibilidade de contar mais histórias de marcas brasileiras. Imagina não ser brasileiro e não reparar no rodinho de pia? A celebração da brasilidade foi o norte para a capa, o título, as cores, a curadoria de artigos e, claro, para a experiência memorável que a gente quer que a revista seja. Aqui a gente não coloca impresso no mundo para ir parar no fundo da gaveta. Ou é para guardar, ou é para expor, ou é para interagir. Ou quem sabe até todas as anteriores. É por isso que, dessa vez, ela tem uma lombada quadrada (fica melhor na estante) , tem uma página que vira pôster (um lembrete para a sua área de trabalho) e tem um álbum de figurinhas. _ Brasilidade + impresso + offline + Copa do Mundo. A cada quatro anos essas referências se encontram na sensação de completar, uma de cada vez, dezenas de páginas de um álbum. As figurinhas, por sua vez, trazem imagens conhecidas, reconhecidas, algumas até icônicas, que representam o melhor do país naquela modalidade. A nossa modalidade é o marketing. A nossa seleção, portanto, é composta de ações de marcas que destacam o melhor da criatividade brasileira nas últimas décadas. Fiquem agora com a nossa Seleção, na certeza de que ela deixou grandes destaques de fora. Porém com a esperança de que isso gere bons debates e trocas. _ Em 2013, a Kombi contava em primeira pessoa as histórias reais que as pessoas enviaram para celebrar a sua despedida. Em 1998, a Johnson’s Baby reforçava a sua linha de shampoos infantis, e oferecia a trilha sonora para milhões de banhos de bebês dali em diante. Em 2019, o McDonald’s deixava de lado a consistência em nome do seu real significado (e grafia) para o público brasileiro. Em 1997, dois pequenos esquimós transformavam Danoninho em sorvetinho, e a gente ganhava uma frase para repetir por décadas. Em 2025, a Red Bull transformava um edifício icônico de Porto Alegre em rampa para um dos maiores skatistas do Brasil. Em 2011, alguns pôneis cantavam em volta de um carro Nissan , em um dos virais mais marcantes do início das redes sociais. Em 2020, a Netflix esgotava em algumas horas uma edição especial impressa do seu universo de conteúdo. Em 1991, uma série de conteúdos transformava uma marca em adjetivo e fazia muita gente se questionar se qualquer coisa era ou não era “assim uma Brastemp ”... Em 2025, o Canva colocou a Xuxa em um dos seus figurinos icônicos para lançar uma linha de produtos e uma campanha especial “para adultinhos”. _ Além de uma Seleção de Campanhas, a Revista Bits to Brands tem 50 páginas de conteúdo e ilustrações. Ela é a materialização da nossa identidade visual e conteúdo, e também daquilo que a gente acredita: o poder das palavras, a conexão para além das telas e o valor que as coisas ganham quando passam a fazer parte da vida real de alguém. Para viabilizar o seu envio para diferentes cantos do Brasil, estamos fazendo uma tiragem especial em forma de produto social. Você pode garantir a sua pelo valor de R$ 79,90 - e todo o lucro desta ação será destinado a uma ONG de incentivo à leitura no Brasil. Esperamos que seja uma boa leitura, uma ótima surpresa e algo significativo e duradouro como só o impresso é capaz de se tornar. Sem mais delongas: EU QUERO UMA REVISTA (é só clicar no botão - enquanto durar o estoque) para inspirar, com O Boticário #publi ✨ A nova linha Nativa SPA Ameixa Intensa foi anunciada com uma mescla de conteúdo orgânico, influenciadores e até ameixas gigantes. E O Boticário mostrou que uma boa estratégia de comunicação acontece entre o online e o offline, agregando ao entretenimento ao invés de interrompê-lo. Durante a novela Quem Ama Cuida, a marca foi inserida em meio a dois personagens que representam o seu principal atributo: intensidade. Na cena, amostras do novo hidratante são usadas e mencionadas de forma sutil. Só no break comercial que a mensagem se completa: dobro de ameixa, dobro de amostras nas lojas. E o link com oferta vai para as redes sociais minutos depois. Ou seja: quando cada canal cumpre o seu papel, a conexão emocional acontece, o produto se faz presente e a promoção aparece na hora certa. para ler com calma 📄 As marcas que souberam aproveitar a trend dos anos 80 Tudo que a Apple lançou na semana passada A última edição da Revista Gama, sobre memória “Quando você decide que quer filmar ou tirar foto, sua atenção está se voltando a quê? visualFeast.title: #303 | Marcas multiespécie
visualFeast.description: nas edições anteriores #301 | O legado da Copa do Mundo 2026 #302 | Os oráculos da timeline tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Segundo o estudo Tendências Brasil 2026, de Globo Gente: Pela primeira vez, casais com filhos são menos da metade das famílias do país; Lares unipessoais, casais com pets e uniões homoafetivas cresceram vertiginosamente; O número de pessoas que moram sozinhas triplicou de 2000 para 2022. _ É neste contexto que os animais de estimação têm ganhado status (e padrão de vida) de filhos em muitas casas brasileiras. Plano de saúde, guarda-roupas para todas as estações do ano, festas de aniversário, creches e escolas, entretenimento… Em uma economia que que movimenta um estimado de R$ 77 bilhões por ano. Quando novas configurações de família são cada vez mais “multiespécie”, esses códigos passam a fazer parte da comunicação de todo tipo de categoria. Todo mundo percebeu que falar com “pais de pet” é estratégico na busca pela atenção, cada vez mais escassa, e da conexão emocional, cada vez mais dispersa. O fator “fofo” é capaz de reter as pessoas por mais tempo, enquanto gera uma reação imediata - curtir, comentar, compartilhar e, claro, comprar. Segundo dados da Buzzmonitor, o aumento no engajamento com publicações que contém pets é de 16%. É por essas e outras que temos visto pets em todos os lugares. De montadoras de carro a fast-food (sim). Sendo público-alvo de novos produtos, influenciadores das suas causas ou apenas “bichinhos propaganda”. O movimento que impulsionou o crescimento de diversas empresas do segmento pet, agora atinge todas as que sabem aproveitá-lo. Marcas que estão se tornando multiespécie. _ O Grupo Boticário levou a sua experiência em perfumaria e desenvolvimento de produtos para uma marca dedicada a deixar a rotina com cães e gatos mais cheirosa. A Stanley lançou o Pet Bowl, feito do mesmo material dos seus produtos que retém temperaturas, para manter a água dos bichinhos gelada e evitar o uso de plástico no seu dia a dia. A Rimowa agora também tem a Pet Carrier Bag, uma bolsa para transporte de animais até 8kg que, além do cuidado no conforto e design, é feita para se acoplar às malas da marca. Até o McDonald’s está pensando no bem-estar desses membros da família. Não lanches especiais (ainda), mas com uma embalagem lançada em Singapura - a Happy Meow Bag é um brinquedo para gatos inspirado nos pacotes do restaurante. _ E talvez o maior sinal das mudanças em como representamos “família” e a inclusão dos pets na estratégia das mais diversas marcas, esteja no segmento de carros. Houve um tempo em que falar de SUVs era sinônimo de imagens de carros grandes com crianças no banco de trás e muitas malas indo pegar a estrada. Hoje, quem está sendo transportado é o cachorro. Ano passado, para lançar o novo modelo da Tracker, a Chevrolet trouxe o vira-lata caramelo como protagonista da sua campanha. Além do filme publicitário, aproveitou o hype do filme Caramelo, na Netflix, para ações em redes sociais. E essa semana mesmo, a Peugeot lançou o E-5008 Dog Edition, com funcionalidades e acessórios focados no conforto dos pets. _ Basicamente, depois de criar uma indústria inteira em torno de si, os animais de estimação agora estão conquistando espaço em marcas de todos os segmentos. Pets atraem o olhar, inspiram emoção e tornam qualquer comunicação mais memorável. Mas a sua presença é mais do que um atalho no jogo da atenção. Ela é reflexo de um novo contexto social e uma nova ideia de família. Num presente que deixa isso cada vez mais evidente, e um futuro que não mostra qualquer sinal de que isso mude. E nenhuma marca quer ficar no passado. para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Em meio a tantas marcas buscando rejuvenescer, usando inclusive a nostalgia pra atrair os mais jovens, o Burger King faz um aceno claro aos “boomers” - até no nome. O combo “Boomer King”, lançado na França, convida as pessoas que cresceram entre os anos 80 e 90 a revisitarem a sua juventude. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 Em todos esses anos de Bits to Brands, os livros são presença constante. Entre recomendações ora semanais aqui, ora ocasionais na timeline; e uma curadoria individual e também colaborativa, centenas de títulos já passaram por aqui. Aproveitamos as novas features da Amazon para organizar a nossa biblioteca em listas com links diretos. Só de marketing e branding são vinte. acesse a nossa nova biblioteca _ Falando em livros, na última semana teve Festival Literário em Paraty. Além da autora mais vendida do evento, Socorro Acioli ofereceu o que é provavelmente um dos melhores depoimentos sobre como reagir a críticas. _ Em parceira com a Porto Rocha, o Tinder foi descobrir se é possível “ser um aplicativo de relacionamentos que não tenta conversar com todo mundo, mas ainda passar a sensação de que é para todo mundo”. graphicDesign.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
graphicDesign.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. References The film Creativity in the Age of AI , Space10, directed by Joss Fong and Áron Filkey: youtube.com/watch?v=y7g-nRooZr8 Space10 Studio: space10.com Highlights of nine years of work: space10.com/highlights Inside Ikea’s Innovation Lab for the Future of Home Design, Fast Company , 2015: fastcompany.com/3053873 Selected Space10 projects worth a look Products of Place: Localised Design with AI - How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Tomorrow’s Meatball : Visualising the future of food, including the dogless hotdog. Future Food Today : a Space10 cookbook of recipes built around alternative ingredients. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. Spaces on Wheels : a study of what driverless cars could become once they’re more than transport. graphicDesign.title: Designer Portraits: Susan Kare ⌘ The woman who gave the computer a face
graphicDesign.description: Good design is not about what medium you are working in. It’s about thinking hard about what you want to do and what you have to work with before you start. — SK Susan Kare joined Apple in 1982 as the sole creator of screen graphics in the Macintosh group. As the designer “ who gave the Macintosh a smile ” she is best known for developing the distinctive icons, typefaces, and other pixel elements that gave the Macintosh its characteristic look and feel. A sculptor picks up graph paper In 1982, Susan Kare was living in the Bay Area, welding a life-size razorback hog for a museum in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Her father, Morley Richard Kare, had founded the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, spending his career studying taste and smell. His daughter had a PhD from NYU, a background in sculpture and fine art, and zero experience with computers. Then Andy Hertzfeld called. Hertzfeld and Kare had known each other since they were fourteen, classmates at Harriton High School outside Philadelphia. He was now the lead software architect on a secret project at Apple: the Macintosh. He needed someone to design the icons and typefaces for its screen. He told her if she got some graph paper, she could make small images. Kare went to the University Art supply store in Palo Alto and bought a $2.50 sketchbook. That sketchbook now sits in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Susan Kare. Apple Macintosh OS icon sketchbook. 1982 — MoMa She went to the Palo Alto public library, checked out every book she could find on typography, and brought them to the interview to prove she knew something about type. “I went into it totally green” she said later. Apple offered her a fixed-length contract to design fonts and icons. In January 1983, she started working at Apple. Her business card read “Macintosh Artist.” Susan Kare, Apple's “Macintosh Artist” relaxes at her desk in 1984. Photographer: Norman Seeff 1,024 squares The Macintosh used a bit-mapped display. The display controlled every pixel on screen. Kare’s canvas was a 32-by-32 pixel grid. 1,024 squares to communicate a single idea. She understood the constraint immediately. “Bitmap graphics are like mosaics and needlepoint and other pseudo-digital art forms, all of which I had practiced before going to Apple,” she said. “I didn’t have any computer experience, but I had experience in graphic design.” No icon editor existed when she started. She learned to calculate the hex equivalent of her pixel drawings so Hertzfeld could keyboard them into the prototype. He built her a proper editor that generated hex values under the icons. Eventually she used MacPaint itself to create icons. A MacPaint screenshot featuring Kare’s artistry, 1983. Notice the icon menu at left and the Chicago system font used for the pull-down menus. Some icons already existed from the Lisa, Apple’s earlier computer. The arrow cursor. The document with a folded corner. The trash can. The Lisa’s interface was functional but clinical, icons designed by engineers to label functions, not to invite use. It also used non-square pixels, so every element needed reworking for the Mac’s display. Kare refined the trash can. She created the application icon, a hand holding a pencil against a diamond shape, to distinguish apps from documents. She designed the Happy Mac, the smiling face that greeted users at startup. She designed the ticking bomb that appeared during system failures. For the copy function, she tried drawing a photocopier. Then she drew a cat looking in a mirror. Copy cat. She scrapped it because it wouldn’t translate internationally. The lasso, the paint bucket, the paintbrush. Each icon went through rounds of sketching on graph paper before touching a screen. Her process was the same as any visual designer working in any medium in any century. Pencil, paper, iteration. The screen was just the final surface. Kare's Happy Macintosh icon appeared at startup, greeting users with a smile to let them know everything was okay. She designed warmth into a machine. Fonts in 9 by 7 dots Most digital typefaces in 1983 were monospaced. Every character occupied the same width. Kare wanted proportional fonts, letters that breathed according to their natural shape. Each letter had to fit in a grid of 9 by 7 dots. The bold system font started as “Elefont.” It became Chicago, the typeface that would appear on the Macintosh and later the iPod for over twenty years. Kare and Hertzfeld named the early fonts after commuter train stops on Philadelphia’s Main Line: Overbrook, Merion, Ardmore, Rosemont, Paoli. Steve Jobs told them the names were too parochial. He wanted world-class cities. The fonts became New York, Geneva, London, Toronto, Venice. One font, Ransom, looked like cutout letters from a kidnapper’s note. Jobs renamed it San Francisco. Another, Cairo, featured tiny pictograms: a palm tree, a crescent moon, a skateboard. Decades before Apple introduced emoji, Kare had already drawn proto-emojis into a font. The command key and the Swedish campground ⌘ Every keyboard needs a modifier key. The Mac team struggled to find the right symbol for theirs. Kare found the answer in Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook, a reference she kept at her desk at Apple. The symbol marked interesting features on Swedish campgrounds. It was abstract enough to work as a keyboard glyph, meaningful enough to carry intention. It became ⌘, one of the most recognized symbols in computing. The pirate flag Steve Jobs liked to tell the Mac team: “ It’s better to be a pirate than join the navy. ” When the team moved into a new building, Bandley 3 , programmer Steve Capps wanted a flag. He asked Kare to design one. She drew a Jolly Roger with the eyepatch replaced by Apple’s rainbow logo. They flew it over the entrance. It stayed there for over a year. At one point, the Lisa team stole it. In 2016, Apple flew the flag again to mark the company’s 40th anniversary. This wallpape r is a nod to the Jolly Roger that flew over Bandley 3 in 1983, the building the Mac team worked in as they put the finishing touches on the Macintosh. Apple recently flew a recreation of the original 1983 flag in 2016 , when it celebrated its 40th anniversary on April 1st, shortly before moving its HQ from Infinite Loop to Apple Park. And the flag is still available on Susan Kare's website . After the Mac The Macintosh shipped in January 1984. The entire visual language Kare created came from roughly one year of work. When Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985, Kare followed him to NeXT as creative director. She was one of the company’s first ten employees. At NeXT, she connected Jobs with one of her design heroes. Kare was a devoted Paul Rand fan. She introduced Jobs to Rand’s books, and together they hired Rand to design the NeXT logo. Kare and David Kelley visited Rand at his studio. Rand, then in his seventies, told them: “I’ve been doing this for fifty-five years, and I know what you should do.” Susan Kare, center, was a creative director at NeXT, and she left with Jobs after his ouster at Apple. Kim Jenkins, right, was a key member of the NeXT marketing team. Kare founded her own studio, Susan Kare LLP, in 1989. Over the next three decades, she designed interface elements for Microsoft, Oracle, Facebook, IBM, and Sony Pictures. She designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. In 2003, she served on the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, designing coins for the United States Mint. In 2015, she joined Pinterest as product design lead. In 2018, AIGA awarded her the AIGA Medal, one of the profession’s highest honors. Kare designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. The proof of concept The Museum of Modern Art calls Kare “a pioneering and influential computer iconographer.” The label misses the point. She made the Macintosh feel human and had never touched a computer before Apple hired her. She came from sculpture, fine art, mosaics, needlepoint. She treated the pixel grid the same way she treated any design surface: as a constraint that shapes the work. “I hoped to help counter the stereotypical image of computers as cold and intimidating,” Kare said. Someone with a $2.50 sketchbook and a sculptor’s eye decided that the visual language of technology should borrow from the one humans already knew. That turned out to be enough. “I still spend my days turning dots on and off.” Today, Kare is working as a design architect at Niantic Labs and still runs her own studio in San Francisco. She sells limited-edition signed prints of her icon work, collaborates with brands like Ledger on pixel art for hardware , and her original 1982 sketchbooks remain on display at MoMA. Needlepoint to Ledger Nano™: A Conversation with Susan Kare Apple turns 50 this year. ( 50 years of thinking different. ) Researching Susan Kare felt like walking back to where it all started; reading about how she approached design problems, how she collaborated, how she used constraints to shape the work. They built the foundations of how we use computers today. They had constraints on their screens but none in their minds. I hope you enjoyed reading this one. graphicDesign.description: nas edições anteriores #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 A essa altura você já sabe que a Bits to Brands virou uma revista impressa . Duas, na verdade, considerando que estamos na segunda edição. Já somos praticamente uma banca. O que você talvez não saiba é que este processo criativo começou lá em 2014, quando a gente visualizou uma revista impressa que viria com um boné, feita para ser a companhia ideal para o verão de 2025. (Por isso a garota da capa estava sentada em uma cadeira de praia lendo uma revista, que dentro tinha uma página só de palavras cruzadas e vinha com um cartão postal retratando um dia de praia…) Ou seja: não basta selecionar os artigos, ordenar e diagramar de forma que faça sentido e pensar o projeto gráfico - toda revista precisa ter um tema. _ Na sua segunda edição, em 2026, o escolhido foi Bora de Brasil . Uma das grandes tendências do ano, e um tema de grande interesse por aqui - das pesquisas traduzindo a nossa cultura à possibilidade de contar mais histórias de marcas brasileiras. Imagina não ser brasileiro e não reparar no rodinho de pia? A celebração da brasilidade foi o norte para a capa, o título, as cores, a curadoria de artigos e, claro, para a experiência memorável que a gente quer que a revista seja. Aqui a gente não coloca impresso no mundo para ir parar no fundo da gaveta. Ou é para guardar, ou é para expor, ou é para interagir. Ou quem sabe até todas as anteriores. É por isso que, dessa vez, ela tem uma lombada quadrada (fica melhor na estante) , tem uma página que vira pôster (um lembrete para a sua área de trabalho) e tem um álbum de figurinhas. _ Brasilidade + impresso + offline + Copa do Mundo. A cada quatro anos essas referências se encontram na sensação de completar, uma de cada vez, dezenas de páginas de um álbum. As figurinhas, por sua vez, trazem imagens conhecidas, reconhecidas, algumas até icônicas, que representam o melhor do país naquela modalidade. A nossa modalidade é o marketing. A nossa seleção, portanto, é composta de ações de marcas que destacam o melhor da criatividade brasileira nas últimas décadas. Fiquem agora com a nossa Seleção, na certeza de que ela deixou grandes destaques de fora. Porém com a esperança de que isso gere bons debates e trocas. _ Em 2013, a Kombi contava em primeira pessoa as histórias reais que as pessoas enviaram para celebrar a sua despedida. Em 1998, a Johnson’s Baby reforçava a sua linha de shampoos infantis, e oferecia a trilha sonora para milhões de banhos de bebês dali em diante. Em 2019, o McDonald’s deixava de lado a consistência em nome do seu real significado (e grafia) para o público brasileiro. Em 1997, dois pequenos esquimós transformavam Danoninho em sorvetinho, e a gente ganhava uma frase para repetir por décadas. Em 2025, a Red Bull transformava um edifício icônico de Porto Alegre em rampa para um dos maiores skatistas do Brasil. Em 2011, alguns pôneis cantavam em volta de um carro Nissan , em um dos virais mais marcantes do início das redes sociais. Em 2020, a Netflix esgotava em algumas horas uma edição especial impressa do seu universo de conteúdo. Em 1991, uma série de conteúdos transformava uma marca em adjetivo e fazia muita gente se questionar se qualquer coisa era ou não era “assim uma Brastemp ”... Em 2025, o Canva colocou a Xuxa em um dos seus figurinos icônicos para lançar uma linha de produtos e uma campanha especial “para adultinhos”. _ Além de uma Seleção de Campanhas, a Revista Bits to Brands tem 50 páginas de conteúdo e ilustrações. Ela é a materialização da nossa identidade visual e conteúdo, e também daquilo que a gente acredita: o poder das palavras, a conexão para além das telas e o valor que as coisas ganham quando passam a fazer parte da vida real de alguém. Para viabilizar o seu envio para diferentes cantos do Brasil, estamos fazendo uma tiragem especial em forma de produto social. Você pode garantir a sua pelo valor de R$ 79,90 - e todo o lucro desta ação será destinado a uma ONG de incentivo à leitura no Brasil. Esperamos que seja uma boa leitura, uma ótima surpresa e algo significativo e duradouro como só o impresso é capaz de se tornar. Sem mais delongas: EU QUERO UMA REVISTA (é só clicar no botão - enquanto durar o estoque) para inspirar, com O Boticário #publi ✨ A nova linha Nativa SPA Ameixa Intensa foi anunciada com uma mescla de conteúdo orgânico, influenciadores e até ameixas gigantes. E O Boticário mostrou que uma boa estratégia de comunicação acontece entre o online e o offline, agregando ao entretenimento ao invés de interrompê-lo. Durante a novela Quem Ama Cuida, a marca foi inserida em meio a dois personagens que representam o seu principal atributo: intensidade. Na cena, amostras do novo hidratante são usadas e mencionadas de forma sutil. Só no break comercial que a mensagem se completa: dobro de ameixa, dobro de amostras nas lojas. E o link com oferta vai para as redes sociais minutos depois. graphicDesign.title: #303 | Marcas multiespécie
graphicDesign.description: nas edições anteriores #301 | O legado da Copa do Mundo 2026 #302 | Os oráculos da timeline tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Segundo o estudo Tendências Brasil 2026, de Globo Gente: Pela primeira vez, casais com filhos são menos da metade das famílias do país; Lares unipessoais, casais com pets e uniões homoafetivas cresceram vertiginosamente; O número de pessoas que moram sozinhas triplicou de 2000 para 2022. _ É neste contexto que os animais de estimação têm ganhado status (e padrão de vida) de filhos em muitas casas brasileiras. Plano de saúde, guarda-roupas para todas as estações do ano, festas de aniversário, creches e escolas, entretenimento… Em uma economia que que movimenta um estimado de R$ 77 bilhões por ano. Quando novas configurações de família são cada vez mais “multiespécie”, esses códigos passam a fazer parte da comunicação de todo tipo de categoria. Todo mundo percebeu que falar com “pais de pet” é estratégico na busca pela atenção, cada vez mais escassa, e da conexão emocional, cada vez mais dispersa. O fator “fofo” é capaz de reter as pessoas por mais tempo, enquanto gera uma reação imediata - curtir, comentar, compartilhar e, claro, comprar. Segundo dados da Buzzmonitor, o aumento no engajamento com publicações que contém pets é de 16%. É por essas e outras que temos visto pets em todos os lugares. De montadoras de carro a fast-food (sim). Sendo público-alvo de novos produtos, influenciadores das suas causas ou apenas “bichinhos propaganda”. O movimento que impulsionou o crescimento de diversas empresas do segmento pet, agora atinge todas as que sabem aproveitá-lo. Marcas que estão se tornando multiespécie. _ O Grupo Boticário levou a sua experiência em perfumaria e desenvolvimento de produtos para uma marca dedicada a deixar a rotina com cães e gatos mais cheirosa. A Stanley lançou o Pet Bowl, feito do mesmo material dos seus produtos que retém temperaturas, para manter a água dos bichinhos gelada e evitar o uso de plástico no seu dia a dia. A Rimowa agora também tem a Pet Carrier Bag, uma bolsa para transporte de animais até 8kg que, além do cuidado no conforto e design, é feita para se acoplar às malas da marca. Até o McDonald’s está pensando no bem-estar desses membros da família. Não lanches especiais (ainda), mas com uma embalagem lançada em Singapura - a Happy Meow Bag é um brinquedo para gatos inspirado nos pacotes do restaurante. _ E talvez o maior sinal das mudanças em como representamos “família” e a inclusão dos pets na estratégia das mais diversas marcas, esteja no segmento de carros. Houve um tempo em que falar de SUVs era sinônimo de imagens de carros grandes com crianças no banco de trás e muitas malas indo pegar a estrada. Hoje, quem está sendo transportado é o cachorro. Ano passado, para lançar o novo modelo da Tracker, a Chevrolet trouxe o vira-lata caramelo como protagonista da sua campanha. Além do filme publicitário, aproveitou o hype do filme Caramelo, na Netflix, para ações em redes sociais. E essa semana mesmo, a Peugeot lançou o E-5008 Dog Edition, com funcionalidades e acessórios focados no conforto dos pets. _ Basicamente, depois de criar uma indústria inteira em torno de si, os animais de estimação agora estão conquistando espaço em marcas de todos os segmentos. Pets atraem o olhar, inspiram emoção e tornam qualquer comunicação mais memorável. Mas a sua presença é mais do que um atalho no jogo da atenção. Ela é reflexo de um novo contexto social e uma nova ideia de família. Num presente que deixa isso cada vez mais evidente, e um futuro que não mostra qualquer sinal de que isso mude. E nenhuma marca quer ficar no passado. para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Em meio a tantas marcas buscando rejuvenescer, usando inclusive a nostalgia pra atrair os mais jovens, o Burger King faz um aceno claro aos “boomers” - até no nome. wild.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
wild.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. wild.title: Out There
wild.description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. In a place you know, reflect on “ what that place has witnessed , remembered, celebrated, protected, or survived. … If this river, tree, park, or wooded pathway could talk — tell us poems, tell us stories — what do you think it would say?” Write about it. Leave a comment THERE’S MORE! In connection with Write Out, there are two online events that sound cool: Hawaiian Kilo: Writing Rooted in Place Native Hawaiians developed a practice known as Kilo — “to watch, observe, examine, or forecast.” This means closely observing the natural world and its patterns, ideally to better steward the environment. A Zoom workshop, “led by teachers from the Waiākea Intermediate School in Hilo Hawai'i,” happens October 13, 2026, 6 pm US Central time . Details and (free) registration here . Haiku + Comic = Haikomic The Write Time with Write Out Ambassador Grant Snider on October 20 . Snider is a writer/artist who combines haiku with comics. (Details on that here , and at his newsletter. ) And he is this year’s Write Out Author Ambassador. Check the Write Out newsletter for event details as they emerge. I really like the sound of this and hope to revisit. Grant Snider, via Incidental Comics Leave a comment PS I was a Write Out Ambassador last year. I love Write Out! Seriously. Thank you! Subscribe now THE NEXT FREE EDITION IN TWO WEEKS! IN OTHER NEWS David Lee Roth , EMT . “ Reading Maps plots the routes characters travel in novels and films — you can trace the Pequod’s ocean path as it chases Moby Dick, or Victor Frankenstein’s pursuit of his monster from Geneva to the Arctic.” — Recomendo Lighthouses of the World , a digital map. Via Popular Science . “What Gertrude Stein, T. S. Eliot and Joan Didion Really Meant With Their Most Famous Aphorisms .” The International Dada Archive collects scanned Dada pamphlets from the early 20th century. Mark Frauenfelder found one in English called The Blind Man , co-edited by Marcel Duchamp. Its second issue, from 1917, covered the controversy around Duchamp’s Fountain , a urinal he submitted under the name Richard Mutt to the Society of Independent Artists exhibition. wild.title: #306 | Uma seleção de campanhas
wild.description: nas edições anteriores #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 A essa altura você já sabe que a Bits to Brands virou uma revista impressa . Duas, na verdade, considerando que estamos na segunda edição. Já somos praticamente uma banca. O que você talvez não saiba é que este processo criativo começou lá em 2014, quando a gente visualizou uma revista impressa que viria com um boné, feita para ser a companhia ideal para o verão de 2025. (Por isso a garota da capa estava sentada em uma cadeira de praia lendo uma revista, que dentro tinha uma página só de palavras cruzadas e vinha com um cartão postal retratando um dia de praia…) Ou seja: não basta selecionar os artigos, ordenar e diagramar de forma que faça sentido e pensar o projeto gráfico - toda revista precisa ter um tema. _ Na sua segunda edição, em 2026, o escolhido foi Bora de Brasil . Uma das grandes tendências do ano, e um tema de grande interesse por aqui - das pesquisas traduzindo a nossa cultura à possibilidade de contar mais histórias de marcas brasileiras. Imagina não ser brasileiro e não reparar no rodinho de pia? A celebração da brasilidade foi o norte para a capa, o título, as cores, a curadoria de artigos e, claro, para a experiência memorável que a gente quer que a revista seja. Aqui a gente não coloca impresso no mundo para ir parar no fundo da gaveta. Ou é para guardar, ou é para expor, ou é para interagir. Ou quem sabe até todas as anteriores. É por isso que, dessa vez, ela tem uma lombada quadrada (fica melhor na estante) , tem uma página que vira pôster (um lembrete para a sua área de trabalho) e tem um álbum de figurinhas. _ Brasilidade + impresso + offline + Copa do Mundo. A cada quatro anos essas referências se encontram na sensação de completar, uma de cada vez, dezenas de páginas de um álbum. As figurinhas, por sua vez, trazem imagens conhecidas, reconhecidas, algumas até icônicas, que representam o melhor do país naquela modalidade. A nossa modalidade é o marketing. A nossa seleção, portanto, é composta de ações de marcas que destacam o melhor da criatividade brasileira nas últimas décadas. Fiquem agora com a nossa Seleção, na certeza de que ela deixou grandes destaques de fora. Porém com a esperança de que isso gere bons debates e trocas. _ Em 2013, a Kombi contava em primeira pessoa as histórias reais que as pessoas enviaram para celebrar a sua despedida. Em 1998, a Johnson’s Baby reforçava a sua linha de shampoos infantis, e oferecia a trilha sonora para milhões de banhos de bebês dali em diante. Em 2019, o McDonald’s deixava de lado a consistência em nome do seu real significado (e grafia) para o público brasileiro. Em 1997, dois pequenos esquimós transformavam Danoninho em sorvetinho, e a gente ganhava uma frase para repetir por décadas. Em 2025, a Red Bull transformava um edifício icônico de Porto Alegre em rampa para um dos maiores skatistas do Brasil. Em 2011, alguns pôneis cantavam em volta de um carro Nissan , em um dos virais mais marcantes do início das redes sociais. Em 2020, a Netflix esgotava em algumas horas uma edição especial impressa do seu universo de conteúdo. Em 1991, uma série de conteúdos transformava uma marca em adjetivo e fazia muita gente se questionar se qualquer coisa era ou não era “assim uma Brastemp ”... Em 2025, o Canva colocou a Xuxa em um dos seus figurinos icônicos para lançar uma linha de produtos e uma campanha especial “para adultinhos”. _ Além de uma Seleção de Campanhas, a Revista Bits to Brands tem 50 páginas de conteúdo e ilustrações. Ela é a materialização da nossa identidade visual e conteúdo, e também daquilo que a gente acredita: o poder das palavras, a conexão para além das telas e o valor que as coisas ganham quando passam a fazer parte da vida real de alguém. Para viabilizar o seu envio para diferentes cantos do Brasil, estamos fazendo uma tiragem especial em forma de produto social. Você pode garantir a sua pelo valor de R$ 79,90 - e todo o lucro desta ação será destinado a uma ONG de incentivo à leitura no Brasil. Esperamos que seja uma boa leitura, uma ótima surpresa e algo significativo e duradouro como só o impresso é capaz de se tornar. Sem mais delongas: EU QUERO UMA REVISTA (é só clicar no botão - enquanto durar o estoque) para inspirar, com O Boticário #publi ✨ A nova linha Nativa SPA Ameixa Intensa foi anunciada com uma mescla de conteúdo orgânico, influenciadores e até ameixas gigantes. E O Boticário mostrou que uma boa estratégia de comunicação acontece entre o online e o offline, agregando ao entretenimento ao invés de interrompê-lo. Durante a novela Quem Ama Cuida, a marca foi inserida em meio a dois personagens que representam o seu principal atributo: intensidade. Na cena, amostras do novo hidratante são usadas e mencionadas de forma sutil. Só no break comercial que a mensagem se completa: dobro de ameixa, dobro de amostras nas lojas. E o link com oferta vai para as redes sociais minutos depois. Ou seja: quando cada canal cumpre o seu papel, a conexão emocional acontece, o produto se faz presente e a promoção aparece na hora certa. para ler com calma 📄 As marcas que souberam aproveitar a trend dos anos 80 Tudo que a Apple lançou na semana passada A última edição da Revista Gama, sobre memória “Quando você decide que quer filmar ou tirar foto, sua atenção está se voltando a quê?
